notes.meaning: Samuel poured oil on Saul's head to show that God had chosen him to lead Israel. Anointing was an outward sign of God giving a person special gifts and authority for an office. Samuel then kissed Saul to show personal respect, affection, and loyalty to the new king. Israel was called the Lord's inheritance, meaning the people still belonged to God and Saul was only a servant leading under Him.

other.label: Catholic
other.view: Early Christian writers like Augustine noted that kings anointed with oil were shadows pointing ahead to Jesus, the true Christ or Anointed One.

notes.meaning: Samuel gave Saul three precise signs to prove that this call to be king really came from God. The first sign would happen near the tomb of Saul's ancestor Rachel, which reminded him that earthly glory ends in the grave. The two men he met would tell him the lost donkeys were found and that his father was now worried about his safety.

Saul would next meet three men carrying sacrifices of young goats, bread, and wine on their way to worship God at Bethel. The men would greet Saul as a friend and give him two loaves of their bread. This gift was a quiet foretaste of the tribute paid to a king, and it reminded Saul to stay humble and remember the time he received bread from strangers.

Samuel told Saul to go next to Gibeah of God, a town where the enemy Philistines had an army outpost. There he would meet a group of prophets coming down from the place of worship with harps, tambourines, flutes, and lyres. These prophets were students of God's law who praised God and sang songs under the Holy Spirit's guidance.

God's Holy Spirit would come upon Saul with great power, leading him to join the prophets in praise. This divine touch would transform Saul into a different person. Instead of having the quiet thoughts of a farmer, he would be given the bravery, wisdom, and dignity needed to lead a nation.

Once all these predicted events took place, Saul could move forward with total confidence that God was with him. Samuel encouraged him to act wisely and boldly as opportunities arose. Seeing God's word come true would give him the courage to step into public leadership.

Samuel gave Saul instructions to go down to Gilgal and wait seven full days for him to arrive. Samuel would offer the sacred sacrifices and tell Saul what God wanted him to do. This showed that even though Saul was king, he still had to obey God's prophet and wait on God's timing.

As soon as Saul turned to leave Samuel, God changed Saul's heart and gave him new desires and abilities for leadership. Just as Samuel had foretold, every single sign happened that very day. God proved to Saul that His word can always be trusted.

differ.view: God changed Saul's heart in a civic sense to fit him for governing, not in a saving sense of personal regeneration.
Saul received a genuine spiritual gift of holiness and wisdom, but later lost it through his own sin and disobedience.

notes.meaning: Saul and his servant arrived at Gibeah, and the company of prophets met them just as Samuel had said. The Spirit of God came powerfully upon Saul, and he immediately joined them in ecstatic praise. God gave him the freedom and joy to sing and worship alongside them.

The people from Saul's hometown were astonished when they saw him praising God with the prophets. They knew his family and knew he had never studied with the prophets before. Their surprise shows how suddenly and visibly the Spirit had changed his behavior.

A man in the crowd answered by asking who gives the prophets their gifts. He meant that God is the true father and teacher of all prophets, so He can give His Spirit to anyone He chooses, including Saul. From this event, the question became a popular proverb used whenever someone turned up in an unexpected holy role.

When Saul finished prophesying, he went up to the local high place of worship. He likely went there to pray and give thanks to God for fulfilling all the signs. It showed a desire to seek God's presence as his life began to change.

Saul's uncle asked him and his servant where they had been during their long absence. Saul gave a truthful and direct answer, explaining that they had looked everywhere for the donkeys and finally went to Samuel for help.

Saul's uncle was curious and pressed him to share everything the famous prophet had said. Saul told him about the donkeys being found, but kept the matter of the kingdom completely secret. By keeping quiet, Saul showed humility and wisdom, choosing to wait for God to reveal him publicly.

Samuel summoned the tribes of Israel to meet before the Lord at Mizpah. This was the place where God had previously granted Israel a major victory through prayer. Samuel brought them there so the choice of a king would be made in God's presence.

Samuel spoke for the Lord, reminding the Israelites how God had delivered them from Egypt and protected them from all their oppressors. He told them plainly that demanding a human king was a rejection of God, who had always saved them from trouble. Even so, Samuel told them to stand before the Lord by their tribes and clans to receive their king.

Samuel cast lots to reveal God's choice to the entire nation. The lot first pointed to the small tribe of Benjamin, then to the family of Matri, and finally to Saul himself. But when the people looked around to celebrate, Saul was nowhere to be found.

The people asked the Lord whether Saul had even arrived at the gathering. The Lord answered that Saul was hiding among the supply wagons and baggage. Saul hid because he felt unworthy, nervous, and overwhelmed by the heavy call to lead the nation.

The people ran and brought Saul out of his hiding place into the middle of the crowd. When he stood among them, he was a head taller than everyone else. His impressive height made him look like the exact kind of strong leader the people had wanted.

Samuel presented Saul to the crowd, pointing out that there was no one like him in all Israel. The people shouted with joy, wishing long life and prosperity to their newly chosen ruler. They gladly accepted him as their king.

Samuel explained the laws and rights of the kingdom so both the king and the people would know their boundaries. He wrote these rules on a scroll and placed it before the Lord for safe keeping. Afterward, Samuel sent everyone home in peace.

Saul returned quietly to his home in Gibeah without demanding a grand palace or royal court. A group of brave men went with him to act as his guard and support his authority. These men stood by Saul because God had moved their hearts to do what was right.

Some rebellious men refused to accept Saul, mocking his background and asking how he could possibly save them. They showed their disrespect by refusing to bring him customary gifts of honor. Saul chose to hold his peace and say nothing, showing patience and self-control in the face of insult.
